Rodrigo, thanks for taking the call. I'll get straight to the point. Can we end our contract with our distributor in Brazil next month?
Possibly. But let me probe a little before I answer. What happened? Did they break the contract?
No, not at all. Their sales are fine. It's just that our new CEO wants a change.
I see. Who made that decision? And who else knows about it?
He made it last week, and only the board knows. Well, the board and an online retailer in São Paulo. He's been talking to them for months.
Then I won't beat around the bush. Is the real question how to end this contract, or how to start selling online without a fight?
Honestly? The second one. I didn't want to put you on the spot with the whole story in the first five minutes.
That's fine. Can you elaborate on one thing? Didn't the distributor sign an exclusivity clause with you?
They did, in 2022. And that's our underlying concern. If they're exclusive, can we even talk to the retailer?
That's exactly what we need to get to the bottom of. Send me the contract today, and I'll call you on Thursday with an answer.
Before I answer, can I ask a few follow-up questions?
What happened, exactly?
Is that the real question, or is there something behind it?

I've been a family doctor for twenty years, and the most important thing I've learned is that the first question is rarely the real one. A patient comes in and asks about a pain in her knee. We talk about the knee for ten minutes. Then, with her hand on the door handle, she says, 'Oh, and one more thing.' And that one more thing is the reason she came. So now I ask follow-up questions early. I don't ask, 'Is that all?', because people always say yes. I ask, 'What else is worrying you today?' It's an open-ended question, and it gives people permission to talk. I also ask, 'Who sent you here?' or 'What made you call this week, and not last month?' Something happened this week. Someone said something. When I find out what it was, the visit takes the same time, but it's a completely different visit. My patients don't hide things from me on purpose. They're just waiting for the right question.

I've interviewed politicians on the radio for twenty-five years, and young reporters always ask me the same thing: how do you prepare your questions? The truth is that I prepare only the first one. The interview happens in the second question. A politician answers the first question with a speech he has practiced at home. My job is to listen for the one word that doesn't fit. If he says, 'Mistakes were made,' I ask, 'Who made them?' If he says, 'We spoke to the community,' I ask, 'Who did you speak to? And when?' Short questions work best, because long questions give people time to escape. And I never ask two questions at once, because people always answer the easy one. One more thing: silence. When an answer stops too early, I don't say anything for three seconds. Very often, the most interesting sentence of the whole interview comes right after that silence.
